name: Injera
summary: Spongy, tangy fermented flatbread with a honeycomb surface, the edible plate for every Ethiopian stew.
story: Injera is the everyday bread of Ethiopia and Eritrea, traditionally made from teff, a tiny local grain. It is cooked on one side only on a large clay or metal griddle, and serves as plate, spoon and food at once. Meals are served on a large round of injera with stews placed on top and extra rolled alongside.

steps.title: Start the batter
steps.text: Whisk the teff flour and 600 ml water in a large non-metal bowl into a smooth, thin batter like pancake batter. Cover loosely with a cloth and leave at room temperature (22 to 26 C) for 2 to 3 days.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Stir once a day. The batter is ready when it has bubbles on top, smells pleasantly sour like yoghurt or sourdough, and a clear amber liquid has risen to the top. Pour off this liquid and discard.

steps.title: Make the absit
steps.text: Take 60 ml of the batter and whisk with the boiling water in a small pot. Cook over low heat, stirring, for 2 minutes until it thickens to a paste. Cool completely.

steps.title: Combine and rest
steps.text: Stir the cooled paste and the salt back into the batter. Rest 1 hour. The batter should be thin and pourable, like single cream; add a little water if thick.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.text: Heat a large non-stick frying pan or crepe pan over medium heat. It is hot enough when a drop of water dances and evaporates quickly. Do not oil the pan.

steps.title: Pour the batter
steps.text: Pour about 120 ml batter in a spiral, starting from the outside and moving to the centre, then quickly swirl the pan to cover the base. Tilt so the batter is a thin even layer.

steps.title: Cook one side
steps.text: Bubbles will form and burst across the surface, leaving small holes called eyes. Cover with a lid and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the top is dry and the edges lift easily from the pan; do not flip.

steps.title: Cool flat
steps.text: Slide the injera onto a clean cloth or tray, holes up, in a single layer. Let it cool fully before stacking or it will stick together. Repeat with the rest of the batter.

tips: Use filtered or boiled-and-cooled water if your tap water is heavily chlorinated; it can slow fermentation.
A very sour batter can be softened with a pinch of baking soda before cooking.
If no eyes form, the batter is too thick or the pan too cool; if it browns, the pan is too hot.
Teff is expensive and hard to find. Many cooks outside Ethiopia blend it with other flours (see swaps).

swaps.swap: Use half teff and half plain or self-raising flour with a little sparkling water; the injera is milder and softer but not gluten-free.
Add 1 tbsp live plain yoghurt and ferment 24 hours in a warm place for a quicker, less complex sourness.
